questions.q: What is a vCPU, accurately speaking?
options: A dedicated physical core reserved permanently for one VM
A time-sliced share of a physical core that the hypervisor's scheduler hands out among VMs
A separate physical chip installed only for virtualization
A feature that only exists in Type 2 hypervisors
questions.explain: A vCPU is not a dedicated core — it's a slice of time on a real physical core, scheduled by the hypervisor across multiple VMs.

questions.q: What problem do Intel VT-x and AMD-V (hardware-assisted virtualization) solve?
options: They add more physical RAM to the host automatically
They let the hypervisor handle privileged CPU instructions directly in hardware instead of slow software emulation
They allow VMs to run without any hypervisor at all
They are only used for networking, not CPU, virtualization
questions.explain: Before VT-x/AMD-V, hypervisors had to software-emulate privileged instructions (binary translation), which was slow. These CPU extensions trap and handle those instructions in hardware.

questions.q: What is a virtual disk, such as a VMDK or VHDX file, really?
options: A separate physical hard drive dedicated to one VM
A single large file on the host's filesystem that the guest OS sees and uses as its own hard drive
A type of network-attached storage device
A feature only available in cloud environments, not on-premises
questions.explain: A virtual disk is just a file on the host filesystem (VMDK for VMware, VHD/VHDX for Hyper-V) that the guest OS treats as a real drive.

questions.q: What is the difference between thick and thin provisioning of a virtual disk?
options: Thick reserves the full disk size on the host up front; thin only grows the file as the guest actually writes data
Thick is only available on Linux; thin only on Windows
There is no real difference between the two options
Thin provisioning is always faster than thick provisioning for every workload
questions.explain: Thick provisioning reserves the full size immediately; thin provisioning lets the virtual disk file grow only as data is actually written, packing more VMs onto limited storage.

questions.q: How does memory overcommit work in a hypervisor?
options: It physically adds more RAM chips to the server while it is running
It assigns VMs more total virtual RAM than the host physically has, relying on not all VMs using their full allocation simultaneously
It deletes unused VMs to free up RAM permanently
It is only possible with Type 2 hypervisors
questions.explain: Because not every VM uses its full memory allocation at the same instant, hypervisors can overcommit virtual RAM and reclaim unused memory from one VM to give to another via techniques like ballooning.
